questions.question: What is PostgreSQL and why does it exist as a deep subject? It is a mature, open-source relational database with a reputation for standards compliance, extensibility, and advanced features (JSON, indexes, concurrency) that rival commercial DBs.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL ('Postgres') is a mature, open-source object-relational database management system known for standards compliance (SQL), reliability, extensibility, and advanced features — complex indexes, full-text search, JSON/JSONB, geospatial (PostGIS), and strong concurrency (MVCC) — that rival commercial databases. It exists as a deep subject because these features, and the trade-offs behind them (index types, isolation levels, query planning), decide whether a Spring Boot app is fast and correct under real load, not just whether it stores rows.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Postgres as a feature-rich relational DB whose advanced capabilities (MVCC, index types, JSONB, EXPLAIN) you must know to tune a real backend, not just 'it runs SQL'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Postgres as 'just SQL' — unaware of MVCC, index types (B-tree, GIN, GiST), EXPLAIN/ANALYZE, or isolation levels, which is where real performance and correctness live.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the capabilities that make Postgres deep — MVCC for concurrency, index types (B-tree/GIN/GiST), JSONB for semi-structured data, EXPLAIN/ANALYZE for planning, isolation levels for correctness — and connect each to a real consequence for a Spring Boot app.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: PostgreSQL ('Postgres') is a mature, open-source object-relational database management system, widely used and known for SQL standards compliance, reliability, extensibility, and advanced features that rival commercial databases: complex index types (B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN), full-text search, JSON/JSONB for semi-structured data, geospatial support (PostGIS), and strong concurrency via MVCC. It exists as a deep subject because these features — and the trade-offs behind them (which index, which isolation level, what the query planner does) — decide whether a Spring Boot app is fast and correct under real load. Treating Postgres as 'just SQL' misses where performance and correctness actually live.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) — readers don't block writers and vice versa; each transaction sees a snapshot, enabling high concurrency; (2) index types — B-tree (equality/range), GIN (array/JSONB/full-text), GiST (geospatial/range), BRIN (large ordered tables); choosing the right one is the core tuning lever; (3) JSONB — binary JSON for semi-structured data, queryable and indexable, a middle ground between relational and document; (4) the query planner and EXPLAIN/ANALYZE — understanding the plan (seq scan vs. index scan vs. join strategy) is how you find slow queries; (5) isolation levels — read committed (default) to serializable, trading consistency for concurrency; (6) ACID and WAL — durability via write-ahead logging; (7) extensibility — types, functions, extensions (PostGIS).

sections.title: Postgres Features and What Each Solves
rows: Must read the plan, not guess

sections.title: MVCC, index choice, and EXPLAIN in a Spring Boot context
sections.content:
-- MVCC: readers see a snapshot; writers create a new row version.
--   No read/write blocking, but dead versions accumulate -> VACUUM reclaims.

-- Index choice decides lookup speed:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user  ON orders(user_id);                 -- B-tree: equality/range
CREATE INDEX idx_tags ON products USING GIN (tags);              -- GIN: array membership
CREATE INDEX idx_attrs ON products USING GIN (attrs jsonb_path_ops); -- GIN: JSONB containment

-- Query: find products tagged 'java' with attrs.price < 100.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE tags @> ARRAY['java'] AND (attrs->>'price')::int < 100;
-- READ the plan: a Seq Scan means the index isn't used (wrong type/missing);
--   a Bitmap Index Scan means GIN is used. The plan, not intuition, tells
--   you what to fix. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it for real costs.

-- Isolation: default READ COMMITTED is fine for most; SERIALIZABLE retries
--   on conflict for correctness-critical flows (e.g., account transfers).
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is performance versus correctness: stronger isolation (serializable) guarantees correctness but causes serialization failures you must retry; lower isolation (read committed) is faster but allows non-repeatable reads and phantom rows. A second tension: indexes speed up reads but slow writes and consume space, so over-indexing is a real cost — index only what queries need. The third: JSONB gives you a document model inside Postgres (a middle ground), but querying and indexing JSONB is less efficient than a normalized relational design for highly relational data — use it for genuinely semi-structured fields, not to avoid schema design.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Postgres is a feature-rich open-source RDBMS; its advanced features (MVCC, index types, JSONB, EXPLAIN) are where real performance and correctness live.
MVCC lets readers not block writers (snapshot per transaction), enabling high concurrency but requiring VACUUM to reclaim dead versions.
Index types matter: B-tree for equality/range, GIN for array/JSONB/full-text, GiST for geospatial, BRIN for large ordered tables.
EXPLAIN/ANALYZE shows the query plan — reading it, not guessing, is how you find and fix slow queries.
Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency: read committed (default, fast) to serializable (correct, with retries).
JSONB offers a document model inside Postgres — a middle ground for semi-structured fields, not a replacement for normalized relational design.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: PostgreSQL is a mature, open-source relational database, and it's a deep subject because its advanced features — not just 'it runs SQL' — are what decide whether a Spring Boot app is fast and correct under real load. The capabilities I anchor on: MVCC, multi-version concurrency control, which lets readers not block writers by giving each transaction a snapshot, enabling high concurrency at the cost of bloat that VACUUM reclaims. The index types — B-tree for equality and range, GIN for arrays and JSONB and full-text, GiST for geospatial — because choosing the right index is the core tuning lever. JSONB, which gives you a queryable, indexable document model inside Postgres as a middle ground for semi-structured fields. EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which shows the actual query plan, because reading the plan rather than guessing is how you find slow queries. And isolation levels, which trade consistency for concurrency — read committed is the fast default, serializable is correct for things like account transfers but throws serialization failures you must retry. The trade-off I always name is performance versus correctness, and the cost of indexes: they speed up reads but slow writes and consume space, so I index only what queries actually need.

questions.question: How do MySQL and PostgreSQL compare for Java backend developers, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.title: MySQL vs PostgreSQL for Java Developers
questions.direct_answer: Both are first-class relational databases with equal Spring Data JPA and Hibernate support, so the choice is about edges, not baseline. **PostgreSQL wins on types** (JSONB, arrays, ranges, PostGIS), SQL-standard compliance, transactional DDL, and MVCC without gap locks. **MySQL wins on operational ubiquity** — Aurora MySQL, Vitess sharding, and simpler binlog replication dominate very-high-write workloads. For a fresh Spring Boot service, default to PostgreSQL unless team operational experience or write volume tips you toward MySQL/Aurora.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason about database selection as a set of concrete trade-offs — type system, replication, tooling, and cloud managed services — instead of expressing a preference, and whether you understand what actually changes in a Spring Boot application when you swap engines.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Answering with a personal preference or listing superficial differences (port numbers, licenses) without connecting them to real Spring Boot decisions like Hibernate dialect, JSONB mapping, or transactional DDL in Flyway migrations.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how PostgreSQL's MVCC avoids MySQL Repeatable Read's gap-lock deadlocks, name one or two extensions (PostGIS, TimescaleDB, pgvector, Citus) you'd reach for, and describe the narrow scenarios where Aurora MySQL still wins — for example massive simple-schema write throughput.

sections.title: Two Mature Engines with Different Sweet Spots
sections.content:
MySQL and PostgreSQL are both ACID, open-source, and fully supported by Spring Data JPA/Hibernate.
- For a standard CRUD service they are interchangeable — swap the driver, the dialect, the JDBC URL, and most applications run unchanged.
- The differences matter at the edges: **type system**, **SQL compliance**, **replication model**, and **operational ecosystem**.

PostgreSQL's MVCC never holds gap locks, its planner supports more join algorithms (hash, merge, nested-loop, parallel), and its type system (JSONB, arrays, ranges, enums, custom types, domain constraints) frequently removes whole tables that MySQL would need for the same modelling. MySQL's ecosystem — Aurora, Vitess, ProxySQL, PlanetScale — is the most battle-tested at extreme scale.

The interview signal is not which you prefer but whether you can map a workload to the database that removes the most friction.

sections.title: Feature Matrix — MySQL 8 vs PostgreSQL 16
sections.content:
| Dimension | MySQL 8 | PostgreSQL 16 |
|---|---|---|
| SQL standards compliance | Good, some deviations | Excellent, most compliant |
| JSON | `json` type, limited indexing | `jsonb` + GIN, full operator suite |
| Arrays / ranges / enums | Not native | Native, first-class |
| Full-text search | Basic built-in | `tsvector`/`tsquery` + GIN |
| Geospatial | Basic spatial types | PostGIS (industry standard) |
| Window functions | Supported | Supported + more frame options |
| CTEs | `WITH` and `WITH RECURSIVE` | Same, optimizer fences removed in PG 12+ |
| MVCC | Undo log + gap locks at RR | Versioned tuples, no gap locks |
| Transactional DDL | No (DDL auto-commits) | Yes (DDL rolls back) |
| Replication | Binlog (row/statement/mixed) | WAL streaming + logical replication |
| Sharding | Vitess, ProxySQL | Citus, partitioning |
| Managed options | RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, PlanetScale | RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon, Crunchy |
| Hibernate dialect | `MySQLDialect` | `PostgreSQLDialect` |
| Default port | 3306 | 5432 |

sections.title: Decision Framework — Five Scenarios Where the Choice Matters
sections.content:
**Scenario 1 — Schema-flexible attributes**
- PostgreSQL JSONB with a GIN index answers `WHERE attrs @> '{"color":"red"}'` in microseconds against millions of rows
- MySQL JSON requires generated columns with B-tree indexes per queryable field, which means each new filter is a schema migration
- Pick PostgreSQL when a meaningful fraction of the model is schema-flexible (product attributes, feature flags, integration payloads, multi-tenant config)

**Scenario 2 — Geospatial or time-series**
- PostGIS is the open-source standard for spatial joins, radius queries, geofencing, raster operations
- TimescaleDB hypertables add continuous aggregates and incremental refresh for time-series workloads
- MySQL spatial exists but is strictly less capable

**Scenario 3 — Hybrid OLTP/OLAP on the same node**
- PostgreSQL's parallel query, partial indexes, BRIN, recursive CTEs, and rich window frames fit reporting-on-transactional better
- Tables under ~500 GB with analytical queries often stay in PostgreSQL instead of a separate warehouse

**Scenario 4 — Extreme write throughput on simple schema**
- Very-high-volume logging, ingestion, or simple CRUD at massive scale benefits from MySQL/InnoDB
- Aurora MySQL's distributed storage layer and Vitess's mature sharding stack remain the default at companies ingesting billions of rows per day

**Scenario 5 — Serverless or edge-first architecture**
- PlanetScale (MySQL, schema branching) and Neon/Supabase (PostgreSQL, serverless cold-start) have different feature ceilings
- Cloud offering often matters more than engine choice at this tier

**For Spring Boot specifically**
- Engine swap is roughly a 30-minute change: driver dependency, `spring.datasource.url`, Hibernate dialect, run migrations on the target
- The hidden tax is engine-specific features you adopted — JSONB, PostGIS, Aurora failover behaviour, MySQL stored procedures — so stay portable until you have a reason not to

sections.title: Switching a Spring Boot Service from MySQL to PostgreSQL
Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When PostgreSQL helps:**
- Rich types (JSONB, arrays, ranges, enums, custom types) collapse side tables
- MVCC without gap locks removes a whole class of deadlocks common under MySQL Repeatable Read
- Transactional DDL makes Flyway/Liquibase migrations safely reversible
- Extensions (PostGIS, TimescaleDB, pgvector, Citus, pg_trgm) cover geospatial, time-series, vector, distributed, and fuzzy-search workloads without a second system

**When MySQL/Aurora helps:**
- Massive write throughput on simple schemas with mature sharding (Vitess) and routing (ProxySQL)
- Aurora MySQL's distributed log-structured storage beats self-managed PostgreSQL replicas at some scales
- Team has deep operational experience; fewer foot-guns around VACUUM, bloat, and long transactions
- Schema branching workflows via PlanetScale are unmatched on the PostgreSQL side today

**Watch for:**
- MySQL Repeatable Read + gap locks creates deadlocks under concurrent inserts — not a bug, a model difference
- PostgreSQL long-running transactions block VACUUM, causing bloat; MySQL accumulates undo log under similar pressure
- Migration paths both ways exist (pgloader for MySQL→PG, AWS DMS either way) but engine-specific features do not survive the trip

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Engine swap is cheap; engine-specific features are expensive** — the dialect, URL, and driver change in an hour, but JSONB queries, PostGIS, and Aurora failover semantics do not transfer; adopt engine-specific features only when the cost is justified
- **PostgreSQL MVCC avoids gap locks** — under Repeatable Read PostgreSQL relies on snapshot visibility while MySQL takes range gap locks, which is why concurrent-insert deadlocks are more common on MySQL than on PostgreSQL
- **JSONB + GIN is structurally different from MySQL JSON** — `WHERE data @> '{"status":"active"}'` uses an inverted index on every key-value pair; MySQL needs one generated column with a B-tree index per filter, turning every new query into a schema change
- **Transactional DDL changes your migration strategy** — on PostgreSQL a Flyway migration that partially fails rolls back; on MySQL each DDL auto-commits, so partial failures leave a broken schema that must be hand-repaired
- **Hibernate dialect is the only Spring Boot change for plain CRUD** — `PostgreSQLDialect` vs `MySQLDialect`; JPA queries, `@Transactional`, and Spring Data repositories behave identically on both engines

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Both engines are production-grade and both are fully supported by Spring Data JPA — the choice is about which friction you want to remove.

**Where PostgreSQL wins**
- Richer type system: JSONB with GIN indexing, arrays, ranges, enums, custom types — each one removes side tables that MySQL would force you to create
- MVCC without gap locks: Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL uses snapshot visibility, so concurrent inserts do not deadlock the way they do under MySQL Repeatable Read
- Transactional DDL: Flyway migrations can contain multiple DDL statements in one transaction and roll back cleanly on failure; MySQL auto-commits each DDL
- Extensions: PostGIS, TimescaleDB, pgvector, Citus, pg_trgm cover geospatial, time-series, vector, distributed, and fuzzy-search workloads without adding a second system

**Where MySQL wins**
- Operational ubiquity: Aurora MySQL, Vitess, ProxySQL, and PlanetScale are the most battle-tested stacks for very high write throughput and sharding
- Simpler mental model for binlog replication when the deployment is a single primary with a handful of replicas
- PlanetScale's schema branching workflow has no PostgreSQL equivalent yet

**For Spring Boot**
- Swap is a 30-minute change: driver, URL, dialect, rerun migrations
- I default to PostgreSQL for new services and reach for MySQL or Aurora MySQL when the team has strong operational experience or the workload is dominated by simple high-volume writes

questions.question: What are window functions in PostgreSQL? Explain RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG, LEAD with examples.
questions.title: PostgreSQL Window Functions — RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG, LEAD
questions.direct_answer: Window functions compute values across a set of rows **related to the current row** without collapsing them with `GROUP BY`. The `OVER` clause defines the window via `PARTITION BY` (scope) and `ORDER BY` (ordering). **`ROW_NUMBER`/`RANK`/`DENSE_RANK`** handle ranking with different tie semantics. **`LAG`/`LEAD`** access adjacent rows for period-over-period math without self-joins. Frame clauses (`ROWS BETWEEN ...`) power running totals and moving averages with a single query.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can solve ranking, deduplication, and trend-analysis problems with a single window query instead of correlated subqueries or self-joins, and whether you understand the PARTITION BY / ORDER BY / frame-clause pieces of the OVER clause.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing RANK with ROW_NUMBER when ties exist, or filtering on a window-function result in WHERE — window functions run after WHERE, so the filter must be applied in an outer query.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER with tie examples, explain the ROWS vs RANGE frame distinction, and show how a supporting index on (PARTITION BY, ORDER BY) columns avoids a spill-to-disk sort.

sections.title: Window Functions — Row-Level Analytics Without GROUP BY
sections.content:
`GROUP BY` collapses rows into one row per group; **window functions** keep every row visible while computing a value based on a set of related rows. That set — the **window** — is defined by the `OVER` clause: `PARTITION BY` scopes it, `ORDER BY` orders it, and an optional **frame clause** (`ROWS` or `RANGE`) picks a subset relative to the current row.

This one idea replaces a large family of self-joins and correlated subqueries: ranking within a group, running totals, moving averages, year-over-year comparisons, top-N per group, and deduplication of 'latest row per entity' are all one-query patterns with windows.

sections.title: Ranking, LAG/LEAD, and Top-N with Sample Data
sections.content:
-- Sample data
-- employees(id, dept, name, salary)
-- monthly_sales(month, revenue)

-- 1. RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER (tie behaviour)
SELECT
    name, dept, salary,
    RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rnk,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
FROM employees;

-- Two ENG employees tied at 95000:
-- name    | dept | salary | rnk | dense_rnk | rn
-- Alice   | ENG  | 95000  |  1  |     1     |  1
-- Bob     | ENG  | 95000  |  1  |     1     |  2   <- rn always unique
-- Charlie | ENG  | 80000  |  3  |     2     |  3   <- RANK skips, DENSE_RANK does not

-- 2. LAG / LEAD — period-over-period without self-joins
SELECT
    month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue, 1)  OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
    LEAD(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next_month,
    revenue - LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS mom_delta,
    ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month))
          / NULLIF(LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS yoy_pct
FROM monthly_sales
ORDER BY month;

-- 3. Top-1 earner per department (ROW_NUMBER pattern)
SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM (
    SELECT name, dept, salary,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
    FROM employees
) t
WHERE rn = 1;

-- 4. Running total + 7-day moving average (frame clauses)
SELECT date, sales,
       SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY date
                        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
       AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY date
                        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM daily_sales;

-- 5. Deduplication — latest row per user
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT u.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
    FROM user_events u
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

-- 6. Percent-of-total without a second query
SELECT product_id, revenue,
       revenue * 100.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER () AS pct_of_total,
       AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category) AS category_avg
FROM product_revenue;

-- 7. EXPLAIN: ensure an index on (PARTITION BY, ORDER BY) columns
-- so WindowAgg consumes presorted input instead of adding a Sort node
CREATE INDEX idx_sales_dept_salary
    ON employees (dept, salary DESC);

sections.title: Frame Clauses — ROWS vs RANGE and Running Windows
sections.content:
**Default frame when ORDER BY is present**
- `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` — this is what produces a running total when you write `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date)` with no explicit frame
- Without `ORDER BY` in the OVER clause, the default is the entire partition — useful for `SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` which attaches the category total to every row

**ROWS vs RANGE distinction**
- `ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` always means exactly the previous physical row and the current row — positional
- `RANGE BETWEEN '1 day' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` means all rows whose ORDER BY value falls within one day of the current row's value — value-based and can include multiple rows with the same timestamp
- For time-series with multiple events per timestamp, the choice changes the answer

**Common frames**
- `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` — running total
- `ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` — trailing N-row moving average
- `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` — entire partition (needed so `LAST_VALUE` returns the partition's last value, not the current row)

**Execution order trap**
- Window functions run **after** WHERE and GROUP BY but **before** ORDER BY
- You cannot filter on a window result in WHERE; wrap in a CTE or subquery and filter in the outer query
- Do the equivalent of `HAVING` by wrapping in a CTE: `WITH r AS (SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) rn FROM t) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn = 1`

sections.title: Beyond the Basics — NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, FILTER, and Performance
sections.content:
**NTILE(n)**
- Splits rows into N approximately equal buckets — useful for quartile/decile cohort analysis
- `NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC)` assigns 1 to the top 25% spenders

**PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST**
- `PERCENT_RANK()` returns `(rank - 1) / (total_rows - 1)` in the range 0–1
- `CUME_DIST()` returns the proportion of rows with a value `<=` the current row — standard empirical CDF

**FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE**
- `FIRST_VALUE(col)` with the default frame returns the first row of the partition
- `LAST_VALUE(col)` with the default frame returns the **current row's value**, not the partition's last — extend the frame to `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` to get the partition's last value
- `NTH_VALUE(col, 3)` picks the third row in the window

**Aggregate-as-window + FILTER**
- Any aggregate (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`, `STRING_AGG`, `ARRAY_AGG`) becomes a window function with `OVER`
- Combine with `FILTER`: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at)` yields a running count of completed rows per user

**Performance**
- A window function with `PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b` over millions of rows requires sorted input — without a supporting index, the plan adds a `Sort` node that can spill to disk
- An index on `(a, b)` or `(a, b DESC)` lets `WindowAgg` consume presorted input directly — often a 10× improvement
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` will show either `Sort` → `WindowAgg` (needs index) or `Index Scan` → `WindowAgg` (good)

sections.title: When to Use Window Functions
sections.content:
**When they help:**
- Ranking within groups — `RANK`, `DENSE_RANK`, `ROW_NUMBER` replace correlated subqueries
- Running totals, moving averages, and cumulative counts — one query, no self-joins
- Period-over-period math (`LAG`/`LEAD`) — month-over-month or year-over-year in a single pass
- Top-N per group — the `ROW_NUMBER() + WHERE rn <= N` idiom
- Deduplication — 'keep the latest row per user' is a `PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC` + `rn = 1` pattern

**When they hurt:**
- Wrong frame clause produces subtly incorrect answers (e.g. `LAST_VALUE` with default frame)
- Missing supporting index forces a full sort; on a 10M-row table this can spill to disk
- Over-using `PARTITION BY ()` (global window) on huge tables repeatedly sorts the entire table

**Watch for:**
- Window functions execute after WHERE and GROUP BY — filter in an outer CTE
- `DISTINCT` is not allowed inside window function arguments in standard SQL
- PostgreSQL allows `WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)` for ordered-set aggregates like `percentile_cont` — distinct from window functions

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`RANK`, `DENSE_RANK`, `ROW_NUMBER` differ on ties** — `RANK` skips numbers after ties (1,1,3), `DENSE_RANK` does not (1,1,2), `ROW_NUMBER` assigns arbitrary unique integers; pick based on whether gaps are acceptable and whether you need deterministic unique rows
- **`LAG`/`LEAD` eliminate self-joins for adjacent-row math** — `amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` is month-over-month delta in one pass instead of joining the table to itself on `month - 1`
- **Default frame with ORDER BY is `RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO CURRENT ROW`** — that default produces a running total; for moving averages and positional windows use `ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`
- **Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY** — filter on a window result by wrapping in a CTE or subquery and applying the filter in the outer query
- **Index on `(PARTITION BY, ORDER BY)` columns avoids spill-to-disk sorts** — without a supporting index, `WindowAgg` needs a `Sort` step that may spill on large tables; the index lets the planner feed sorted rows directly

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Window functions compute values across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them with GROUP BY. The OVER clause is what makes it a window: PARTITION BY defines the scope, ORDER BY defines the ordering, and an optional frame clause picks a subset relative to the current row.

**Ranking — the tie question**
- ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequential integers regardless of ties
- RANK assigns the same number to ties but skips after them, so 1, 1, 3
- DENSE_RANK assigns the same number to ties and does not skip, so 1, 1, 2
- Use ROW_NUMBER when you need strictly one row per position, RANK or DENSE_RANK when ties should genuinely share a rank

**LAG and LEAD**
- LAG gives the previous row's value, LEAD gives the next — so `amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month)` computes month-over-month delta in one pass, no self-join needed
- `LAG(revenue, 12)` gives you the same month in the previous year for year-over-year comparisons

**Running totals and moving averages**
- `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY date)` is a running total because the default frame with ORDER BY is everything from the start to the current row
- A moving average uses an explicit frame, `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` for a 7-day trailing window

**The common pitfall**
- Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY but before ORDER BY, so you cannot filter on a window result in WHERE
- Wrap in a CTE and filter in the outer query — the 'top 1 per group' pattern is `ROW_NUMBER()` in a CTE plus `WHERE rn = 1` outside

**Performance tip**
- An index on the PARTITION BY and ORDER BY columns lets the planner skip the Sort step; without it, a million-row window function can spill to disk

questions.question: How do you work with JSONB in PostgreSQL and when do you choose JSONB over JSON or normalized columns?
questions.title: PostgreSQL JSONB vs JSON — Operators, Indexing, Decision Tree
questions.direct_answer: `json` stores raw text and re-parses on every read; **`jsonb` stores a parsed binary format**, supports operators (`->`, `->>`, `@>`, `?`, `?&`, `?|`, `#>`), and can be indexed with **GIN for containment queries**. Use `jsonb` for schema-flexible attributes (user prefs, product metadata, integration payloads). Use typed relational columns for data you filter, join, or aggregate on hot paths — typed B-tree indexes always outperform GIN for that. Generated columns let you promote JSONB fields to typed columns as access patterns emerge.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating PostgreSQL as a document database — dumping everything into a single JSONB column, losing type safety, and later finding that hot filters cannot use the index because the query uses `->>` text extraction instead of `@>` containment.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `jsonb_path_ops` for a smaller, faster containment-only GIN index, the JSONPath query language (`@?`, `@@`, `jsonb_path_query`), pg_jsonschema for validation, and the generated-column pattern for promoting hot JSONB fields into typed columns.

sections.title: JSONB — Structured Flexibility Without Leaving Postgres
sections.content:
PostgreSQL ships two JSON types. `json` keeps the input text verbatim and re-parses on every access — useful only when you must preserve whitespace or key order. `jsonb` parses once, stores a decomposed binary format with sorted keys and deduplicated values, supports a rich operator set, and can be GIN-indexed.

For any column you query or update, `jsonb` is the correct choice.
- The remaining question is **when to use JSONB at all vs typed relational columns**.
- The senior answer is both: typed columns for data the application filters, joins, or aggregates on hot paths, and JSONB for the long tail of schema-flexible attributes.
- Generated columns bridge the two — as a JSONB field becomes hot, you promote it to a typed, indexed column without changing the write path.

sections.title: Operators, Indexes, and Containment Queries
sections.content:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    price       NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
    category    TEXT NOT NULL,
    attributes  JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb
);

INSERT INTO products (name, price, category, attributes) VALUES
('Widget Pro', 29.99, 'electronics',
 '{"color":"red", "weight_kg":0.5, "tags":["sale","new"], "in_stock":true}');

-- OPERATOR REFERENCE
-- ->   returns jsonb: attributes -> 'color'      -> '"red"'
-- ->>  returns text:  attributes ->> 'color'     -> 'red'
-- #>   returns jsonb: attributes #> '{specs,cpu}'
-- #>>  returns text:  attributes #>> '{specs,cpu}'
-- @>   containment:   attributes @> '{"color":"red"}'::jsonb
-- <@   contained by:  '{"color":"red"}'::jsonb <@ attributes
-- ?    key exists:    attributes ? 'weight_kg'
-- ?|   any key:       attributes ?| array['color','size']
-- ?&   all keys:      attributes ?& array['color','weight_kg']

-- GIN INDEX VARIANTS
-- Default: supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&; larger index
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs_full ON products USING GIN (attributes);

-- jsonb_path_ops: supports ONLY @>; ~30-50% smaller, 2-3x faster lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs_paths
    ON products USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);

-- Expression index for specific-field equality via ->>
CREATE INDEX idx_products_brand ON products ((attributes ->> 'brand'));

-- USING THE INDEX
-- Containment uses GIN (fastest path)
SELECT name FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"color":"red", "in_stock":true}'::jsonb;

-- Key-existence uses GIN
SELECT name FROM products WHERE attributes ? 'weight_kg';

-- ->> comparison does NOT use the default GIN index; needs expression index
SELECT name FROM products WHERE attributes ->> 'brand' = 'Acme';

-- Update a single key (rewrites entire row per MVCC)
UPDATE products
SET attributes = jsonb_set(attributes, '{color}', '"blue"', true)
WHERE id = 1;

-- Remove a key
UPDATE products SET attributes = attributes - 'tags' WHERE id = 1;

-- Expand JSONB into rows
SELECT name, kv.key, kv.value
FROM products, jsonb_each_text(attributes) AS kv
WHERE category = 'electronics';

-- JSONPath (PG 12+): complex predicates
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE attributes @? '$.tags[*] ? (@ == "sale")';

-- Generated column: promote a hot JSONB field to typed + indexed
ALTER TABLE products
    ADD COLUMN brand TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (attributes->>'brand') STORED;
CREATE INDEX idx_products_brand_typed ON products (brand);

sections.title: Decision Tree — JSONB vs Typed Column vs Hybrid
sections.content:
**Start with three questions per field** - Do every row need this field?
- If yes, lean typed column
- Do you filter, join, or aggregate on this field on hot paths?
- If yes, lean typed column
- Does the shape legitimately vary between rows (per-category product attributes, integration payloads, tenant-specific config)? If yes, lean JSONB

**Default for schema-flexible data → JSONB with `jsonb_path_ops` GIN index**
- Product attributes across many categories, user preferences, feature flags, webhook payloads, audit diffs
- Queries are `@>` containment against a small number of keys per row — `jsonb_path_ops` is the right opclass

**Default for core attributes → typed column**
- `price`, `email`, `status`, `user_id`, `created_at` — present on every row, filtered constantly, aggregated in reports
- Typed B-tree indexes beat GIN on every metric that matters for hot-path reads and writes

**Hybrid pattern — generated columns for promotion**
- Start with JSONB; monitor `pg_stat_statements` for recurring queries against the same JSONB paths
- When a path becomes hot, add a `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (attributes->>'x') STORED` column + B-tree index
- Application writes remain unchanged; reads switch to the typed column, which the planner picks automatically

**Anti-patterns to avoid**
- One JSONB column for everything — you lose type safety, FKs, and most query performance
- Deeply nested structures queried by `->>` through three levels — flatten or promote
- Using `json` instead of `jsonb` because 'it was in a tutorial' — `jsonb` supersedes it for every query use case

sections.title: Schema Validation, Updates, and Spring Boot Integration
JSONB Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- Schema flexibility for sparse or variant attributes across rows
- One table instead of several EAV side tables — easier joins, simpler migrations
- GIN-indexed containment makes attribute filters fast without per-field index proliferation

**When it hurts:**
- `->>` text extraction in WHERE does not use the default GIN index — slow unless you add an expression index
- Every JSONB update rewrites the entire row per MVCC — heavy mutation of a single key is expensive on large JSONB values
- Type safety is deferred to the application or to pg_jsonschema — a typo in a key name yields `NULL`, not an error
- JSONB columns are compressed with TOAST when large — reads decompress the whole column even if you only need one key

**Watch for:**
- Missing GIN opclass — default GIN is larger and slower than `jsonb_path_ops` for the common `@>` case
- Deeply nested shapes — consider denormalizing to a child table once queries traverse more than two levels
- Sort or GROUP BY on JSONB paths without an expression index forces a full scan
- `json` vs `jsonb` — older migrations sometimes chose `json`; migrate to `jsonb` when you start querying it

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`jsonb` beats `json` for every query use case** — `json` re-parses on each read and cannot be GIN-indexed; `jsonb` stores a parsed binary format and supports the full operator suite
- **`@>` containment is the GIN-friendly filter; `->>` text extraction is not** — `WHERE attrs @> '{...}'` uses the GIN index directly; `WHERE attrs->>'brand' = 'Acme'` needs a separate expression index
- **`jsonb_path_ops` opclass is smaller and faster for containment-only queries** — use it when queries are dominated by `@>` and never use `?`, `?|`, or `?&`
- **Hot JSONB fields should be promoted to generated columns** — `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (attrs->>'x') STORED` plus a B-tree index gives typed-column performance without changing the write path
- **Validate shape with `pg_jsonschema` or CHECK constraints** — unchecked JSONB columns drift in structure over years; schema validation catches application bugs at write time, not at report time

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JSONB is PostgreSQL's binary JSON type. Unlike the plain JSON type, which keeps the input text and re-parses it on every read, JSONB parses once at write time, sorts keys, deduplicates values, and supports an operator suite plus GIN indexing.

**Operators you use most**
- `->>` extracts a field as text, used in WHERE for equality filters
- `->` extracts a field as JSONB for further navigation
- `@>` checks containment, `WHERE data @> '{"role":"admin"}'` and this is the operator that benefits from a GIN index
- `?` checks whether a top-level key exists

**Indexing**
- A GIN index with the `jsonb_path_ops` opclass is the default for containment queries — it is smaller and faster than the default opclass
- For equality on a specific extracted field, create an expression index on `(attrs->>'email')`

**JSONB vs typed columns**
- Use JSONB for schema-flexible attributes, product metadata, feature flags, payloads — data whose shape legitimately varies between rows
- Use typed columns for data the application filters, joins, or aggregates on hot paths — price, status, user_id, timestamps
- When a JSONB path becomes hot, promote it to a generated column so you get a typed, indexed view without changing the write path

**Gotchas to mention**
- Every JSONB update rewrites the whole row, which is expensive on very large JSONB values
- Schema drift is real — use pg_jsonschema or a CHECK constraint to validate shape at write time

questions.question: What index types does PostgreSQL support and when do you use each?
questions.title: PostgreSQL Indexes — B-Tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Hash
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL ships five primary index types. **B-Tree** is the default for equality, range, and ordering. **GIN** is an inverted index for JSONB, arrays, and full-text search. **GiST** is a generalized tree for geometric, range, and nearest-neighbour queries. **BRIN** stores one summary per block range — tiny indexes on naturally ordered tables like time-series. **Hash** is equality-only and now crash-safe and replicated. Wrong index type means the index exists but the planner never uses it, so matching the data structure to the access pattern is the core skill.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can match the right index type to a query pattern (equality, range, containment, geometric, nearest-neighbour, time-series) instead of reflexively reaching for B-tree, and whether you understand partial, covering, and expression indexes.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a B-Tree index on a JSONB column, a tsvector column, or a geometry column — the planner cannot use it for the containment, text-match, or geometric operators those types support.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain `jsonb_path_ops` for GIN, the INCLUDE clause for covering indexes, partial indexes for soft-deleted rows, BRIN multi-minmax in PG 14+, and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` as the production-safe build.

sections.title: Match the Index Structure to the Access Pattern
sections.content:
Every PostgreSQL index type is a different data structure: **B-Tree** keeps values sorted, **GIN** is an inverted index mapping each tokenized value to the rows that contain it, **GiST** is a generalized balanced tree supporting overlap and nearest-neighbour operators, **BRIN** stores min/max summaries per block range, and **Hash** maps fixed-size hashes to rowids.

The planner picks a plan based on operators and selectivity — so if your query uses `@>` (JSONB containment) or `@@` (full-text match), only GIN can help. If it uses `&&` (geometric overlap) or `<->` (k-NN distance), only GiST can help. B-Tree is never wrong for equality or range on scalar types, but it is not universally right.

sections.title: Index Type Matrix
sections.content:
| Type | Best for | Operators | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B-Tree (default) | Equality, ranges, ORDER BY | `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'pfx%'` | Medium | Covers ~90% of cases |
| GIN | JSONB, arrays, `tsvector` | `@>`, `?`, `?&`, `?|`, `@@` | Large, slow writes | Use `jsonb_path_ops` for containment-only |
| GiST | Geometric, range, kNN | `&&`, `<<`, `>>`, `@>`, `<->` | Medium | Powers PostGIS; supports lossy index |
| BRIN | Large naturally ordered tables | `=`, `<`, `>` (approximate) | Tiny (~1000× smaller than B-Tree) | Ideal for time-series and append-only logs |
| Hash | Equality on long values | `=` only | Small | Crash-safe and replicated since PG 10 |
| SP-GiST | Non-balanced structures (quad-trees, tries) | Type-specific | Medium | Niche: IP ranges, prefixes |
| Bloom | Many low-cardinality columns filtered in arbitrary combinations | `=` | Small | Probabilistic; requires `bloom` extension |

sections.title: One Example Per Index Type with EXPLAIN
sections.content:
-- 1. B-TREE — equality + range + ordering
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created
    ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42
  AND created_at > now() - interval '30 days'
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_user_created on orders
--   Index Cond: (user_id = 42 AND created_at > ...)
--   (actual time=0.03..0.42 rows=20 loops=1)

-- 2. GIN — JSONB containment and full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_products_attrs_gin
    ON products USING GIN (attributes jsonb_path_ops);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"brand":"Acme","in_stock":true}'::jsonb;
-- Bitmap Heap Scan on products
--   Recheck Cond: (attributes @> ...)
--   -> Bitmap Index Scan on idx_products_attrs_gin
--      Index Cond: (attributes @> ...)

CREATE INDEX idx_articles_fts
    ON articles USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', body));

-- 3. GiST — geometric overlap + nearest-neighbour
CREATE EXTENSION postgis;
CREATE INDEX idx_stores_geom
    ON stores USING GIST (geom);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, name
FROM stores
ORDER BY geom <-> ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(-122.4, 37.8), 4326)
LIMIT 5;
-- Index Scan using idx_stores_geom (kNN)
-- Order By: geom <-> ...

-- 4. BRIN — naturally ordered large tables (time-series)
CREATE INDEX idx_readings_time_brin
    ON sensor_readings USING BRIN (recorded_at)
    WITH (pages_per_range = 32);

-- PG 14+ multi-minmax for data with occasional outliers
CREATE INDEX idx_readings_time_brin_multi
    ON sensor_readings USING BRIN (recorded_at timestamptz_minmax_multi_ops);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*) FROM sensor_readings
WHERE recorded_at BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-07';
-- Bitmap Heap Scan  (recheck)
--   -> Bitmap Index Scan on idx_readings_time_brin
--      Index Cond: (recorded_at BETWEEN ... AND ...)
-- Index size ~5 MB for a 100 GB table

-- 5. HASH — equality on long string keys (crash-safe since PG 10)
CREATE INDEX idx_pages_url_hash
    ON web_pages USING HASH (url);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id FROM web_pages WHERE url = 'https://example.com/very/long/path/...';
-- Index Scan using idx_pages_url_hash
-- (Hash index is smaller than the equivalent B-Tree on long strings;
--  cannot serve range, ORDER BY, or LIKE prefix)

-- BONUS 1: PARTIAL INDEX — index only rows that matter
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_active
    ON orders (user_id)
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL AND status IN ('pending','processing');

-- BONUS 2: COVERING INDEX via INCLUDE — Index Only Scan
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering
    ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)
    INCLUDE (status, total)
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT created_at, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42 AND deleted_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
-- Index Only Scan using idx_orders_covering
--   Heap Fetches: 0   <- touches only the index, never the heap

-- BONUS 3: EXPRESSION INDEX
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (LOWER(email));
-- Enables WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com'

-- PRODUCTION-SAFE BUILD
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_covering
    ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)
    INCLUDE (status, total);
-- Does not block writes; check pg_indexes for INVALID indexes afterwards

sections.title: Partial, Covering, and Expression Indexes — the Force Multipliers
sections.content:
**Partial indexes**
- `CREATE INDEX ... WHERE predicate` indexes only the rows matching the predicate
- Classic uses: `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` (active rows only), `WHERE status = 'pending'` (queue rows), `WHERE tenant_id = 42` (hot tenant)
- Smaller index, lower maintenance cost, and often faster scans because the index matches the query shape exactly

**Covering indexes via INCLUDE**
- Introduced in PostgreSQL 11
- `CREATE INDEX ... ON t(a, b) INCLUDE (c, d)` stores `c` and `d` in the leaf pages without adding them to the search key
- Enables **Index Only Scan** — the plan reads everything from the index and never touches the heap, provided the visibility map is up-to-date

**Expression indexes**
- Index a computed value: `CREATE INDEX ON users (LOWER(email))`
- Required when queries filter on a function of a column — the planner will not use a plain-column index for `WHERE LOWER(email) = ?`

**Multi-column B-Tree left-prefix rule**
- `(a, b, c)` can satisfy `WHERE a = ?`, `a = ? AND b = ?`, `a = ? AND b = ? AND c = ?`
- It cannot satisfy `WHERE b = ?` alone — the leading column must appear in the filter
- Put the most selective equality column first; put range columns (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`) at the end because they prevent use of later columns

**Modern variants worth knowing**
- **Bloom index** (`bloom` extension): probabilistic, covers arbitrary combinations of many low-cardinality columns in one index
- **SP-GiST**: non-balanced structures for IP ranges, prefixes, radix trees
- **BRIN multi-minmax** (PG 14+): handles mostly-ordered data with outliers far better than single-range BRIN

sections.title: Index Maintenance, Bloat, and Production Operations
sections.content:
**`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` is mandatory in production**
- Plain `CREATE INDEX` holds an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration of the build — minutes to hours on large tables, blocking all reads and writes
- `CONCURRENTLY` builds in the background with two table scans and a final validation; writes continue
- On failure you get an `INVALID` index — check `pg_indexes` and drop it before retrying
- Works only outside a transaction block

**Index bloat from MVCC**
- Heavy UPDATE workloads create new index entries per update, leaving the old entries until VACUUM reclaims them
- After months of production traffic an index can be 2–3× its fresh size
- Diagnose with the `pgstattuple` extension or pg_stat_user_indexes
- Fix with `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_name` (PG 12+)

**Finding unused and missing indexes**
- Unused: `pg_stat_user_indexes` with `idx_scan = 0` after weeks of traffic — drop to save disk and write cost
- Missing: `pg_stat_user_tables` with very high `seq_scan` and `seq_tup_read` values — candidates for a new index
- Highest-impact targets: `pg_stat_statements` sorted by `total_exec_time` — real cumulative pain

**Planner cost settings**
- `random_page_cost` defaults to 4.0 which assumes spinning disks; on SSDs setting it to 1.1 makes the planner prefer index scans more aggressively
- `effective_cache_size` should roughly match available OS cache — a too-low value makes the planner avoid indexes

**Working with EXPLAIN**
- `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows actual rows, actual time, and cache-vs-disk block counts
- `Heap Fetches: 0` on an Index Only Scan means the visibility map was current; large values mean you should run `VACUUM` sooner
- `Rows Removed by Filter` on a Seq Scan is the smoking gun for a missing index

sections.title: Index Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When indexes help:**
- Hot read paths with selective filters — one well-chosen index can cut latency 100×
- ORDER BY + LIMIT with a matching B-Tree index avoids sorting
- GIN turns JSONB and full-text search from full scans into sub-second lookups
- Partial indexes shrink hot sets so the index stays in buffer cache

**When indexes hurt:**
- Every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE updates every applicable index — write latency rises with index count
- Unused indexes consume disk, buffer cache, and backup size
- GIN writes are noticeably slower than B-Tree; bulk loads often benefit from dropping and recreating GIN indexes
- Too-specific composite indexes explode in count without covering meaningful query shapes

**Watch for:**
- B-Tree on a JSONB column never gets used by `@>` queries — always `USING GIN`
- Hash indexes cannot serve ranges, LIKE, or ORDER BY — the smallest possible use case
- `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` locks the table — never in production
- Indexes do not store NULLs predictably — consider `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` partial indexes when the column is often NULL

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GIN is required for JSONB `@>` and full-text `@@`** — B-Tree cannot serve multi-value containment or inverted-text queries regardless of how the column is declared
- **GiST is the only index for geometric overlap and nearest-neighbour** — PostGIS queries like `ST_DWithin` and `ORDER BY geom <-> pt` depend on a GiST index to be sub-second
- **BRIN shrinks time-series indexes ~1000×** — on naturally ordered or append-only tables like sensor data or logs, a BRIN index on the timestamp is a few megabytes where the B-Tree would be gigabytes
- **Partial + INCLUDE is the most underused combo** — index only the rows the query cares about and include non-key columns so the plan becomes an Index Only Scan that never touches the heap
- **Always `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in production** — plain CREATE INDEX takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration; CONCURRENTLY lets reads and writes continue; validate with `pg_indexes` for INVALID entries afterwards

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PostgreSQL has five main index types and the right answer depends on what operator the query uses.

**B-Tree** is the default and handles equality, ranges, ORDER BY, and LIKE-prefix queries. It covers most queries you write.

**GIN** is an inverted index — it stores one entry per token and maps tokens to rowids. That makes it the only index that can serve JSONB containment with `@>`, array containment, and full-text search with `@@`. For JSONB, the `jsonb_path_ops` opclass is smaller and faster when you only use `@>`.

**GiST** is a generalized balanced tree that supports overlap and nearest-neighbour operators. It is what PostGIS uses for spatial queries and what range types use for `&&` overlap.

**BRIN** stores a summary per block range instead of per row. On naturally ordered tables — time-series, append-only logs — a BRIN index can be a thousand times smaller than a B-Tree and perform comparably for range queries.

**Hash** is equality-only and since PostgreSQL 10 it is crash-safe and replicated. It wins over B-Tree for strict equality on long string keys like URLs because the fixed hash size is smaller than the full string value.

**Three power tools on top of these**
- Partial indexes index only rows matching a predicate — hot subsets like active rows
- Covering indexes via INCLUDE let you return columns straight from the index without touching the heap
- Expression indexes index computed values like `LOWER(email)`

And in production every index must be built with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` or you hold an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks all reads and writes.

questions.title: PostgreSQL Transaction Isolation Levels — Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL supports **Read Committed (the default)**, **Repeatable Read**, and **Serializable**. All three are implemented on MVCC, so **readers never block writers** and writers never block readers. Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement; Repeatable Read takes one snapshot at transaction start and — unlike the SQL standard — also prevents phantom reads. Serializable uses **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)** to detect dangerous read-write dependency cycles and aborts one transaction with `40001` on conflict, so applications must retry.

sections.title: Isolation Levels on Top of MVCC
sections.content:
Concurrent transactions can observe four classical anomalies: **dirty read** (seeing uncommitted data), **non-repeatable read** (same row, different value on re-read), **phantom read** (same query, new rows on re-run), and **serialization anomaly / write skew** (an outcome no serial order could produce). ANSI SQL defines four isolation levels; PostgreSQL implements three — Read Uncommitted is silently upgraded to Read Committed because MVCC never exposes uncommitted data.

MVCC means every row carries `xmin` (creating transaction) and `xmax` (deleting/updating transaction).
- Reads take a **snapshot** of the set of transaction IDs that were committed at snapshot creation and use that snapshot to decide row visibility.
- Because reads never take shared locks, **readers never block writers** and vice versa — the headline benefit of PostgreSQL concurrency.

sections.title: Anomalies Prevented by Each Level
sections.content:
| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom read | Serialization anomaly / write skew |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read Uncommitted (not supported; behaves as RC) | Prevented | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Read Committed (default) | Prevented | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Repeatable Read | Prevented | Prevented | **Prevented (stronger than SQL standard)** | Possible |
| Serializable | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented via SSI |

**MVCC-specific notes**
- Read Committed takes a new snapshot at each statement start
- Repeatable Read takes one snapshot at transaction start and holds it for the whole transaction
- Serializable adds SSI on top of the Repeatable Read snapshot to detect dangerous dependency cycles

sections.title: Spring Boot — Isolation, FOR UPDATE, and Retry
MVCC Internals and Why Long Transactions Hurt
sections.content:
**Snapshots in one paragraph**
- Every row version has `xmin` (creator) and `xmax` (deleter)
- A transaction's snapshot is the set of transaction IDs committed at snapshot creation
- A row is visible if `xmin` is in that set and `xmax` is not — no reader locks required

**Read Committed**
- Fresh snapshot per statement, which is why two reads of the same row in one transaction can differ
- Correct default for most OLTP — lowest overhead, no retry logic required

**Repeatable Read**
- One snapshot for the whole transaction
- PostgreSQL RR also prevents phantom reads because the snapshot simply cannot see rows with `xmin` greater than the snapshot
- Stronger than the SQL standard's RR, weaker than Serializable (still allows write skew)

**Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**
- Tracks **dangerous read-write dependencies** between concurrent transactions
- If a cycle forms, SSI aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE `40001`
- Low overhead vs lock-based Serializable, at the cost of application retry logic

**The long-transaction problem**
- MVCC keeps every row version potentially visible to any active transaction
- A 30-minute report, a forgotten idle-in-transaction client, or a stuck background job holds back the `xmin` horizon
- VACUUM cannot reclaim any dead tuple possibly visible to that transaction — tables and indexes bloat
- Mitigations: `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, `statement_timeout`, alerts on long transactions in `pg_stat_activity`

**Transaction ID wraparound**
- Transaction IDs are 32-bit; wraparound occurs after ~4 billion transactions
- Autovacuum's freeze pass marks old rows as 'frozen' to avoid wraparound
- Falling behind leads to an emergency shutdown that refuses writes — monitor `age(datfrozenxid)`

sections.title: Choosing a Level
sections.content:
**Read Committed — default**
- Every single-statement transaction (`SELECT`, `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ?`, inserts) is correct
- Multi-statement business logic that reads and then writes the same row should use `FOR UPDATE` or optimistic locking, not a higher level

**Repeatable Read**
- Reports, snapshot-based exports, any read-only operation that does multiple queries and needs them to see the same view of the world
- `readOnly = true` in Spring so the driver advertises the transaction as RR

**Serializable**
- Business invariants that span rows or predicates (write skew: 'at least one on call', 'no more than N bookings for the slot')
- Every caller must handle SQLSTATE 40001 with a bounded retry loop — Spring Retry + `CannotSerializeTransactionException`

**Pessimistic `FOR UPDATE` vs optimistic `@Version`**
- `FOR UPDATE` is simpler when contention is low and rows are small
- Optimistic locking scales further because it holds no DB lock; conflicts are detected at commit and retried by the caller

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **MVCC means readers never block writers** — each transaction sees a snapshot; updates create new row versions while old versions stay visible to transactions that need them
- **PostgreSQL Repeatable Read also blocks phantoms** — MVCC's snapshot simply cannot see rows committed after the snapshot, so unlike MySQL you do not need gap locks, which is why concurrent-insert deadlocks are rarer on PostgreSQL
- **Serializable uses SSI, not locks** — it detects dangerous read-write dependency cycles and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001; every SERIALIZABLE caller must have a retry loop with exponential backoff
- **Write skew is the signature Serializable anomaly** — two transactions each read shared state, make independently valid changes, both commit, and the database ends in a state no serial execution could reach; only Serializable prevents it
- **Long-running transactions block VACUUM and cause bloat** — keep transactions short, set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, and monitor `pg_stat_activity` for sessions older than a few minutes

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PostgreSQL supports three isolation levels on top of MVCC: Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable. The headline property of MVCC is that readers never block writers and writers never block readers — each transaction reads from a snapshot instead of taking shared locks.

**Read Committed — the default**
- Each statement gets a fresh snapshot of committed data, so two reads of the same row in one transaction can return different values
- This is the right default for most OLTP workloads; use FOR UPDATE or optimistic locking inside a Read Committed transaction when you need a read-then-write to be atomic

**Repeatable Read**
- Takes one snapshot at transaction start and holds it for the entire transaction
- Unlike the SQL standard and unlike MySQL, PostgreSQL Repeatable Read also prevents phantom reads because the snapshot cannot see rows inserted after it
- Perfect for reports that run multiple queries and need them all to see the same view of the world

**Serializable**
- Prevents write skew, the anomaly where two transactions read overlapping state, each makes a valid independent change, and both commit into a state no serial execution could produce
- PostgreSQL implements it with Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which detects dangerous read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001
- Every caller must have a retry loop — in Spring, `@Retryable(CannotSerializeTransactionException.class)` with exponential backoff

**The operational pitfall**
- Long-running transactions hold back the xmin horizon and prevent VACUUM from reclaiming dead row versions, which causes table and index bloat
- Keep transactions short, configure `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, and monitor `pg_stat_activity` for stuck sessions

questions.question: How do you implement full-text search in PostgreSQL?
questions.title: PostgreSQL Full-Text Search — tsvector, tsquery, GIN, Ranking
questions.direct_answer: PostgreSQL ships native full-text search via **`tsvector`** (processed document) and **`tsquery`** (search expression), matched with the `@@` operator and indexed with **GIN**. `to_tsvector('english', body)` tokenizes, strips stop words, and stems; a GIN index turns search into sub-second lookups on millions of rows. **`ts_rank`** orders by relevance; `ts_headline` returns highlighted snippets. For datasets under ~10M documents with straightforward keyword search, PostgreSQL FTS removes the operational cost of Elasticsearch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can build a practical FTS pipeline end-to-end: store a tsvector, index it with GIN, query with the right tsquery variant, rank results, and integrate with Spring Data JPA via a native query.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `LIKE '%keyword%'` for search, or calling `to_tsvector` in the query predicate without indexing it — both cause a full table scan because the planner cannot use any index for those expressions.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain lexemes, stemming, and configurations; compare `to_tsquery` vs `plainto_tsquery` vs `phraseto_tsquery` vs `websearch_to_tsquery`; mention `pg_trgm` for fuzzy matching, `unaccent` for diacritics, and when Elasticsearch is still the right tool.

sections.title: Native FTS That Is Often Enough
sections.content:
PostgreSQL full-text search processes documents into **lexemes** — normalized word stems with stop words removed — and stores them in a `tsvector`. A `tsquery` expresses a search with boolean operators and the `@@` operator matches them. A GIN index on the tsvector is what turns 'scan every row' into 'lookup in an inverted index'.

For most applications this removes the need for a separate search service. Elasticsearch still wins for faceted search, dense relevance tuning, distributed scale, and autocomplete, but for keyword search combined with relational filters and joins, PostgreSQL is simpler and cheaper.

sections.title: End-to-End — Generated Column, GIN Index, Ranking, Highlighting
sections.content:
-- 1. Store the processed document as a generated column (auto-updated)
CREATE TABLE articles (
    id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title         TEXT NOT NULL,
    body          TEXT NOT NULL,
    language      REGCONFIG NOT NULL DEFAULT 'english',
    search_vector TSVECTOR GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title, '')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body,  '')), 'B')
    ) STORED,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- 2. GIN index — mandatory for fast search
CREATE INDEX idx_articles_fts ON articles USING GIN (search_vector);

-- 3. Query variants
-- to_tsquery: full syntax with & | ! :* (prefix)
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'postgres & (jsonb | index:*)');

-- plainto_tsquery: ANDs the words for you (user-friendly)
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'postgres jsonb index');

-- phraseto_tsquery: exact phrase (ordered adjacency)
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ phraseto_tsquery('english', 'full text search');

-- websearch_to_tsquery: Google-style: quotes, OR, -exclude
SELECT id, title
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english',
    '"full text search" postgres OR mysql -elasticsearch');

-- 4. Relevance ranking
SELECT id, title,
       ts_rank_cd(search_vector, query, 32) AS rank
FROM articles,
     plainto_tsquery('english', 'postgres jsonb') AS query
WHERE search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- 5. Highlighted snippet
SELECT id, title,
       ts_headline('english', body,
                   plainto_tsquery('english', 'postgres jsonb'),
                   'MaxWords=30, MinWords=15, ShortWord=3') AS snippet
FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'postgres jsonb')
LIMIT 20;

-- 6. EXPLAIN: Bitmap Index Scan on idx_articles_fts
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'postgres');
-- Bitmap Heap Scan on articles
--   Recheck Cond: (search_vector @@ ...)
--   -> Bitmap Index Scan on idx_articles_fts
--        Index Cond: (search_vector @@ ...)

-- 7. Spring Data JPA native query
-- public interface ArticleRepo extends JpaRepository<Article, Long> {
--   @Query(value =
--     "SELECT id, title, ts_rank_cd(search_vector, q) AS rank " +
--     "FROM articles, plainto_tsquery('english', :q) q " +
--     "WHERE search_vector @@ q " +
--     "ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT :limit OFFSET :offset",
--     nativeQuery = true)
--   List<Object[]> search(@Param("q") String q,
--                         @Param("limit") int limit,
--                         @Param("offset") int offset);
-- }

sections.title: Tokens, Stemming, and Configurations
sections.content:
**The pipeline**
- `to_tsvector(config, text)` splits the document into tokens
- Each token is classified by a parser (word, email, URL, numeric)
- A dictionary chain for the configuration stems and filters — `english_stem` reduces 'running' and 'ran' to 'run'
- Stop words (`the`, `is`, `a`) are removed before indexing

**Configurations per language**
- PostgreSQL ships ~20 text-search configurations: `english`, `spanish`, `french`, `german`, `russian`, `simple`, etc.
- Store the language per row and build per-language tsvectors: `to_tsvector(language_column, body)` so each row uses its own stemmer
- Install the `unaccent` extension to normalize diacritics: `café` matches `cafe`

**Weights and ranking**
- `setweight(tsvector, 'A')` attaches one of four weights (A highest, D lowest) to each lexeme
- `ts_rank_cd(vector, query, normalization)` computes cover density ranking — rewards documents where query terms are close together and in high-weight fields
- Normalization flag 32 divides by `1 + log(#unique words)` to prevent long documents from dominating

**Query variants at a glance**
- `to_tsquery` — explicit boolean syntax (`&`, `|`, `!`, `:*` prefix)
- `plainto_tsquery` — treats input as a phrase to AND, no operators
- `phraseto_tsquery` — exact phrase match in order
- `websearch_to_tsquery` — Google-style: `"quoted phrases"`, `OR`, `-negation`

sections.title: Fuzzy Matching, Combined Filters, and When to Reach for Elasticsearch
sections.content:
**Fuzzy search with `pg_trgm`**
- Trigram similarity splits text into 3-character sequences
- `similarity(name, 'Jhonny Aplseed') > 0.3` matches despite typos
- `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (col gin_trgm_ops)` makes `ILIKE '%substring%'` index-backed — the only way to accelerate wildcard-prefixed LIKE in PostgreSQL

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_trgm ON users USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);

SELECT name, similarity(name, 'Jhonny Aplseed') AS score
FROM users
WHERE name % 'Jhonny Aplseed'
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

**Combining FTS with relational filters**
- The strength over Elasticsearch: filter and join in one query

```sql
SELECT a.id, a.title
FROM articles a
JOIN authors u ON u.id = a.author_id
WHERE a.search_vector @@ plainto_tsquery('english', :q)
  AND a.organization_id = :orgId
  AND a.created_at > now() - interval '90 days'
ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(a.search_vector, plainto_tsquery('english', :q)) DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

**When Elasticsearch wins**
- Rich faceted aggregations across many dimensions
- Relevance tuning with learning-to-rank or custom scoring models
- Datasets beyond single-instance PostgreSQL scale (hundreds of millions of documents)
- Autocomplete with edge n-grams at very high throughput

**When PostgreSQL FTS wins**
- Everything else — the complexity of operating a second system rarely pays for itself under 10M documents
- Permissions, tenancy, and joins are trivial because the data never leaves the database
- Transactional consistency: the search index is updated in the same transaction as the row

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When PostgreSQL FTS helps:**
- Existing PostgreSQL database, no second system to operate
- Queries combine keyword match with structured filters, tenant scoping, or joins
- Up to tens of millions of documents on a modest server
- Strong consistency requirements — search is always in sync with the row

**When it hurts:**
- Write-heavy workloads — a GIN index on a frequently updated tsvector column is slower than B-Tree maintenance
- Complex relevance tuning — `ts_rank_cd` is fixed-formula; cannot boost individual fields dynamically or use ML rankers
- Faceted navigation with many dimensions — requires several GROUP BY queries where Elasticsearch does one request

**Watch for:**
- Calling `to_tsvector(...)` in WHERE predicates without an expression index — bypasses any pre-built GIN index
- Forgetting `unaccent` for international content — `café` won't match `cafe`
- Stop-word mismatch when using `simple` config — search retrieves common words and noise
- GIN index build time on huge tables — use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and consider partitioning by date

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`tsvector` + `tsquery` + `@@` + GIN is the whole stack** — the tsvector stores lexemes, the tsquery expresses the search, `@@` matches, and GIN is what makes it fast; without the GIN index every search is a full-table scan
- **Stemming and stop-word removal happen automatically per configuration** — `to_tsvector('english', body)` turns 'running', 'ran', 'runs' into the same lexeme and drops 'the', 'is', 'a'; use per-row `regconfig` for multilingual content
- **`setweight` + `ts_rank_cd` gives weighted relevance ranking** — weight the title 'A' and the body 'B' so title matches score higher; `ts_rank_cd` rewards documents where query terms are close together
- **Prefer `websearch_to_tsquery` for user-facing queries** — supports `"quoted phrases"`, `OR`, and `-exclude` without exposing users to the `&`/`|` tsquery syntax
- **Combine FTS with `pg_trgm` for typo tolerance** — `gin_trgm_ops` turns `ILIKE '%substring%'` into an index-backed operation and `similarity()` supports fuzzy matching, filling the gap where FTS's exact stem matching falls short

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PostgreSQL has native full-text search built around two data types and one operator. `tsvector` is a processed document of lexemes with stop words removed and stems applied. `tsquery` is a search expression with boolean operators. The `@@` operator matches them.

**The practical pipeline**
- Store the tsvector as a generated column so it is always in sync: `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED`
- Create a GIN index on the tsvector column — that is what turns full-table scans into sub-second lookups
- Use `plainto_tsquery` or `websearch_to_tsquery` for user-facing input, `to_tsquery` when you need boolean operators explicitly
- Rank with `ts_rank_cd(vector, query)` and highlight with `ts_headline`

**Weighting matters for quality**
- `setweight` attaches one of four weights to different fields so title hits score higher than body hits
- `ts_rank_cd` uses those weights plus cover density, rewarding documents where query terms are close together

**For multilingual content**
- Store the language per row and build the tsvector with that per-row config so each row uses its own stemmer
- Install the `unaccent` extension to fold diacritics so `café` matches `cafe`

**Fuzzy matching**
- The `pg_trgm` extension supports trigram similarity and accelerates `ILIKE '%substring%'` when combined with a `gin_trgm_ops` index
- Combine it with FTS for typo tolerance that the stemmer cannot provide

**When Elasticsearch is still right**
- Datasets over ~100M documents, rich faceted search, learning-to-rank, or autocomplete at very high throughput
- For everything else, PostgreSQL FTS removes the cost of operating a second search system

sections.title: Why PostgreSQL Needs an External Pool
sections.content:
PostgreSQL uses **one OS process per connection**. Each idle connection consumes memory for its backend plus a slot against `max_connections` (default 100). At 10 microservice instances running 20 HikariCP connections each, you already hit 200 — scale to 50 pods and PostgreSQL refuses new connections.

**PgBouncer** is a tiny, fast connection pooler that sits between application and database.
- The application connects to PgBouncer (port 6432 by convention); PgBouncer maintains a small pool of real PostgreSQL connections and hands one out for the duration of a request.
- With transaction pooling, ~30 server connections can serve ~1,000 concurrent client connections because most of them are idle between transactions.

# pgbouncer.ini — production-oriented starting point

[databases]
; one entry per logical database; host/port target real PostgreSQL
app = host=postgres-primary.internal port=5432 dbname=app

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
admin_users = pgbouncer_admin
stats_users = pgbouncer_stats

; ---- POOL MODE ----
; transaction: server connection held only during a transaction (best for stateless HTTP)
; session: held for entire client session (highest compatibility, less multiplexing)
; statement: released after every statement (breaks transactions, rarely used)
pool_mode = transaction

; ---- SIZING ----
; max client-side connections PgBouncer will accept (app side)
max_client_conn = 1000
; server-side pool per (database, user); start at (cores * 2) + spindles
default_pool_size = 30
; safety valve for bursty traffic above default_pool_size
reserve_pool_size = 10
reserve_pool_timeout = 3
; upper bound per database
max_db_connections = 100
max_user_connections = 100

; ---- TIMEOUTS ----
server_idle_timeout = 300
server_lifetime = 3600
query_wait_timeout = 30
client_idle_timeout = 0
idle_transaction_timeout = 60

; ---- PREPARED STATEMENTS (PgBouncer 1.21+) ----
; enable server-side prepared statement support in transaction mode
max_prepared_statements = 100

; ---- TLS ----
client_tls_sslmode = require
server_tls_sslmode = verify-full
server_tls_ca_file = /etc/ssl/certs/ca.pem

log_connections = 1

log_pooler_errors = 1
stats_period = 60
